title: Purgatory
question: Whether there is a Purgatory
teaching: The Catholic Church teaches that those who die in God's grace and friendship, but who are still imperfectly purified, undergo a final cleansing before entering the joy of heaven. This state (or process) of purification is called Purgatory. It is not a 'second chance' at salvation and it is entirely distinct from hell — everyone in Purgatory is already assured of heaven. It concerns the effects and residue of sin (disordered attachments, unrepaired harm, imperfect love) that remain even after guilt itself has been forgiven.
why: The Church grounds this teaching in the conviction that nothing imperfect can enter directly into the full vision of God (cf. Revelation 21:27), combined with the observation that few people die in a state of perfect love and total detachment from sin. Purgatory is understood as an act of God's mercy, not an additional debt exacted from the sinner: it completes, by grace, the sanctification that Christ's death and resurrection already secured. The Church also points to the ancient and continuous Christian practice of praying for the dead, which only makes sense if the dead can still be aided.

objections.objection: Purgatory has no real basis in Scripture. The clearest text used to support it, 2 Maccabees 12:43-46, comes from a book most Protestants don't accept as canonical, and nothing in the accepted Old and New Testament clearly teaches a post-mortem purification.
objections.reply: Catholic theology doesn't rest the doctrine on a single proof-text but on a convergence of scriptural hints read alongside apostolic Tradition. Paul describes a day when each person's work will be tested by fire, and some will be saved 'but only as through fire,' implying a purifying ordeal after death for those who are nevertheless saved (1 Corinthians 3:11-15). Jesus speaks of sins that will not be forgiven 'in this age or in the age to come,' which implies that some sins can be addressed in the age to come (Matthew 12:32). Paul prays for the mercy of the Lord on Onesiphorus in a way many read as a prayer for someone already deceased (2 Timothy 1:16-18). And 2 Maccabees, even if outside the Protestant canon, still shows that intertestamental Judaism already prayed and made offerings for the dead — a practice the early Church inherited and continued, visible in catacomb inscriptions asking for prayers for the deceased from the 2nd and 3rd centuries onward. For Catholics, Scripture doesn't have to carry the doctrine alone, since Scripture is read within the living Tradition of the Church rather than in isolation.

objections.objection: Purgatory undermines the sufficiency of Christ's atonement. If Jesus' death on the cross fully paid for sin, there should be nothing left for the believer to 'finish' after death. This looks like salvation partly by works.
objections.reply: The Church distinguishes between the guilt of sin (which is what separates a person from God, and which is fully remitted through Christ's atonement, received in justification) and the temporal, formative consequences of sin that can remain in a person even after they are forgiven and reconciled to God. Purgatory doesn't add anything to what Christ accomplished on the cross; it's the ongoing application of his grace, finishing a work of sanctification that is itself entirely a gift. An analogy sometimes used: a forgiven child may still need to unlearn old habits and have their character reshaped by love, even though the relationship itself is already fully restored. Purgatory, in this view, is that reshaping completed in God's presence, not a toll paid to reopen a door Christ already opened.
sources: Catechism of the Council of Trent, on Purgatory
Council of Trent, Decree on Purgatory (1563)

objections.objection: The whole doctrine is really a medieval invention that grew out of the indulgence trade — a fundraising mechanism (like Johann Tetzel's preaching) dressed up as theology, not a genuine part of the apostolic faith.
objections.reply: The abuse of indulgences in the late medieval period was real, and the Church itself eventually corrected it — the Council of Trent explicitly condemned the financial abuses even as it reaffirmed the underlying doctrine of Purgatory. But the doctrine and the abuse are historically separable. Prayer and offerings for the dead appear far earlier than the medieval indulgence controversies: in 2nd- and 3rd-century catacomb inscriptions, in the writings of Tertullian and Cyprian, and in Augustine's account of praying for his mother Monica in the Confessions (written around 397). A corrupt fundraising practice that attached itself to a doctrine centuries later doesn't establish that the doctrine itself was invented for that purpose.
sources: Council of Trent, Decree on Purgatory (1563) and Decree on Indulgences (1563)
